title: Regular Expressions and Splitting Text
summary: Match text with regular expressions and loop over its parts and characters.
intro: `LIKE` only knows `%` and `_`. Regular expressions describe text precisely, like "three digits, a dash, four digits", so you can find it, pull it out, or replace it. Then you split text into rows, one per word or character.
setup:
CREATE TABLE messages (id integer, sender text, body text);
INSERT INTO messages (id, sender, body) VALUES
    (1, 'ana', 'Call me at 555-0142 about the launch #launch'),
    (2, 'ben', 'URGENT: server down, ring 555-0199 #ops #oncall'),
    (3, 'cara', 'Lunch   at  noon?   #food'),
    (4, 'dev', 'This is urgent, need 3 reviews #review'),
    (5, 'eli', 'Thanks  for the   help'),
    (6, 'fay', 'Room 204 is free, not Urgent at all');

steps.title: Matching with regular expressions
steps.body:
Every part of this lesson uses one table, `messages (id integer, sender text, body text)`:

```text
 id | sender |                      body
----+--------+-------------------------------------------------
  1 | ana    | Call me at 555-0142 about the launch #launch
  2 | ben    | URGENT: server down, ring 555-0199 #ops #oncall
  3 | cara   | Lunch   at  noon?   #food
  4 | dev    | This is urgent, need 3 reviews #review
  5 | eli    | Thanks  for the   help
  6 | fay    | Room 204 is free, not Urgent at all
(6 rows)
```

A regular expression is a pattern for text, more precise than `LIKE`. Test one with `text ~ pattern`. `~` is case sensitive, `~*` ignores letter case, and `!~` means "does not match".

```sql
SELECT 'Room 204' ~ '[0-9]+';     -- t
SELECT 'URGENT' ~* 'urgent';      -- t
SELECT 'no digits' !~ '[0-9]';    -- t
```

- `[0-9]` is a character class: any one character from the set. `[a-z]` is one lowercase letter.
- `+` means one or more of the item just before it.
- `{n}` means exactly n of it, so `[0-9]{3}` is three digits in a row.
- `^` and `$` pin the match to the start and the end of the text. Inside a pattern, `^` is not power.

Unlike `LIKE`, a pattern matches anywhere in the text, so there is no `%`. Watch the dot: `.` matches any one character, so write `\.` for a real dot. `substring` from the strings lesson also takes a pattern: `substring(text FROM pattern)` returns the first part that matches, or NULL when nothing does.

```sql
SELECT substring('ring 555-0199 now' FROM '[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}');  -- 555-0199
```

example.title: Messages with a phone number
example.prompt: List the messages that hold a phone number like 555-0142, with the first hashtag in each.
example.code:
SELECT id, sender, substring(body FROM '#[a-z]+') AS first_tag
FROM messages
WHERE body ~ '[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}'
ORDER BY id;
example.output:
id | sender | first_tag
----+--------+-----------
  1 | ana    | #launch
  2 | ben    | #ops
(2 rows)
example.explanation: `[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}` means three digits, a dash, then four digits, so only the bodies of `ana` and `ben` match. `fay` has `204`, but no dash and four more digits after it. In the SELECT list, `#[a-z]+` matches a `#` followed by one or more lowercase letters, and `substring` keeps the first such match: `ben` has two tags, but only `#ops` comes back.

practice.title: Urgent messages
practice.prompt:
List the messages that mention urgent in any letter case, with the first number in each body.

1. Select `id` and `sender` from `messages`.
2. Add `first_number`: the first run of digits in the body, or NULL when it has none.
3. Keep only the messages whose body contains `urgent` in any letter case.
4. Sort by `id`.

Expected output:

```text
 id | sender | first_number
----+--------+--------------
  2 | ben    | 555
  4 | dev    | 3
  6 | fay    | 204
(3 rows)
```
practice.starter:
-- TODO: keep only messages that mention urgent in any letter case,
-- and add the first number in the body as first_number
SELECT id, sender
FROM messages
ORDER BY id;
practice.solution:
SELECT id, sender, substring(body FROM '[0-9]+') AS first_number
FROM messages
WHERE body ~* 'urgent'
ORDER BY id;

tests.stdin: INSERT INTO messages (id, sender, body) VALUES (7, 'gus', 'Urgently need 12 chairs'), (8, 'hal', 'urgent!! call back'), (9, 'ivy', 'Pick up 40 cups, no rush');
INSERT INTO messages (id, sender, body) VALUES (7, 'jo', 'uRgEnt: dial 911 or 555-0100'), (8, 'kim', 'Not important, 7 days left');

hints: `~*` works like `~` but ignores letter case, so it finds URGENT, urgent, and Urgent.
`[0-9]+` matches one or more digits in a row, and `substring` returns the first such run.
A body with no digits gives NULL, which prints as an empty cell.

steps.title: Replacing with regexp_replace
steps.body:
`regexp_replace(text, pattern, replacement)` finds a pattern and swaps in new text. It is like `replace`, but the thing you search for is a pattern instead of fixed text.

By default it replaces only the **first** match. Add the flag `'g'` (global) as a fourth argument to replace every match. Forgetting `'g'` is the classic gotcha:

```sql
SELECT regexp_replace('555-0142', '[0-9]', '#');       -- #55-0142
SELECT regexp_replace('555-0142', '[0-9]', '#', 'g');  -- ###-####
```

A quantifier lets one match cover many characters. `' +'` matches a run of one or more spaces, so replacing it with a single space tidies uneven spacing in one call:

```sql
SELECT regexp_replace('a   b  c', ' +', ' ', 'g');     -- a b c
```

A quantifier applies only to the item just before it: `' {2}'` is two spaces, and `'ab+'` is an `a` then one or more `b`. The original column never changes, because `regexp_replace` returns a new value.

example.title: Masking digits
example.prompt: Show every message with each digit replaced by #.
example.output:
id |                     masked
----+-------------------------------------------------
  1 | Call me at ###-#### about the launch #launch
  2 | URGENT: server down, ring ###-#### #ops #oncall
  3 | Lunch   at  noon?   #food
  4 | This is urgent, need # reviews #review
  5 | Thanks  for the   help
  6 | Room ### is free, not Urgent at all
(6 rows)
example.explanation: `[0-9]` matches one digit, and the `'g'` flag replaces every match, so the whole phone number becomes `###-####`. Rows with no digits come back unchanged. Without `'g'`, only the first digit of each body would turn into `#`.

practice.title: Tidy spacing
practice.prompt:
Show the messages that have two spaces in a row, with every run of spaces collapsed to one space.

1. Select `id` and `sender` from `messages`.
2. Add `tidy`: the body with every run of one or more spaces replaced by a single space.
3. Keep only the messages whose body has two spaces in a row.
4. Sort by `id`.

Expected output:

```text
 id | sender |         tidy
----+--------+----------------------
  3 | cara   | Lunch at noon? #food
  5 | eli    | Thanks for the help
(2 rows)
```
practice.starter:
-- TODO: keep messages with two spaces in a row, and add the tidy column
SELECT id, sender, body
FROM messages
ORDER BY id;
practice.solution:
SELECT id, sender, regexp_replace(body, ' +', ' ', 'g') AS tidy
FROM messages
WHERE body ~ ' {2}'
ORDER BY id;

tests.output:
id | sender |         tidy
----+--------+----------------------
  3 | cara   | Lunch at noon? #food
  5 | eli    | Thanks for the help
(2 rows)

tests.stdin: INSERT INTO messages (id, sender, body) VALUES (7, 'gus', 'Meet    at  the     gate'), (8, 'hal', 'One space only here');
tests.output:
id | sender |         tidy
----+--------+----------------------
  3 | cara   | Lunch at noon? #food
  5 | eli    | Thanks for the help
  7 | gus    | Meet at the gate
(3 rows)

tests.stdin: INSERT INTO messages (id, sender, body) VALUES (7, 'ivy', 'Bring  snacks'); DELETE FROM messages WHERE id = 3;
tests.output:
id | sender |        tidy
----+--------+---------------------
  5 | eli    | Thanks for the help
  7 | ivy    | Bring snacks
(2 rows)

hints: Filter with `~` and the pattern `' {2}'`, which means a space repeated exactly two times.
`' +'` matches one or more spaces, and the `'g'` flag replaces every run, not just the first.

steps.title: Looping over parts and characters
steps.body:
`string_to_table(text, delimiter)` splits text and returns **one row per part**. Like `generate_series`, it goes in FROM, so you get a loop over the pieces without writing a loop.

```sql
SELECT * FROM string_to_table('a-b-c', '-');   -- 3 rows: a, b, c
```

Pass `NULL` as the delimiter to get one row per character instead.

Results only have a guaranteed order with ORDER BY, so you need each part's position to sort by. `WITH ORDINALITY` adds it: a column counting the rows 1, 2, 3 in the order the parts appear in the text. Name both columns with `AS t(part, n)`, the part first and the counter last, then sort by the counter:

```sql
SELECT n, part
FROM string_to_table('a-b-c', '-') WITH ORDINALITY AS t(part, n)
ORDER BY n;
```

Two gotchas. The delimiter is plain text, not a pattern, so `'.'` splits at real dots. Two delimiters in a row give an empty part, so `'a,,b'` splits into three rows. And unlike `split_part`, which returns one piece, this returns all of them as rows you can filter, compute on, and sort.

example.title: Colors and letters
example.prompt: Split a list of colors into numbered rows, then split the word SQL into its characters.
example.output:
n | word
---+-------
 1 | red
 2 | green
 3 | blue
(3 rows)

 n | ch
---+----
 1 | S
 2 | Q
 3 | L
(3 rows)
example.explanation: The first query splits at each comma and makes one row per color. `WITH ORDINALITY` adds the counter, and `AS t(word, n)` names the part `word` and the counter `n`. The second query passes `NULL` as the delimiter, so every character becomes its own row, and `n` is its position in the text.

practice.title: Words and lengths
practice.prompt:
Split a sentence into words, with each word's position and length.

1. Split `'learn sql one step at a time'` at each space with `string_to_table` in `FROM`.
2. Number the words with `WITH ORDINALITY` and name the columns `word` and `n`.
3. Select `n`, `word`, and the word's length as `letters`.
4. Sort by `n`.

Expected output:

```text
 n | word  | letters
---+-------+---------
 1 | learn |       5
 2 | sql   |       3
 3 | one   |       3
 4 | step  |       4
 5 | at    |       2
 6 | a     |       1
 7 | time  |       4
(7 rows)
```

Put the function in FROM, then `WITH ORDINALITY AS t(word, n)`.
`length(word)` works on each row, just like on a column.

recap:
- `~` matches a pattern, `~*` ignores letter case, and `!~` means no match.
- `[0-9]` is a character class, `+` means one or more, and `{n}` means exactly n.
- `substring(text FROM pattern)` returns the first match, or NULL.
- `regexp_replace(text, pattern, replacement)` replaces the first match, and `'g'` replaces them all.
- `string_to_table(text, delimiter)` makes one row per part, and a `NULL` delimiter makes one row per character.
- `WITH ORDINALITY AS t(part, n)` numbers the rows so you can sort by position.
